subtitle_zh: 三位主持人聊婚姻背后的金钱研究：消费倾向、婚前协议、婚礼花费、共同账户与家庭决策权。

turns.en: A tightwad is not someone who doesn't get a lot of pleasure from spending, it's someone who deep down wishes they could get more pleasure from spending than they're actually getting.
turns.zh: 所谓抠门者（tightwad），并不是那种花钱得不到多少乐趣的人，而是内心深处希望自己花钱时能比现在获得更多乐趣的人。

turns.en: Couples who experienced the lowest divorce rates spent less than a thousand dollars on their wedding. My wife will tell you a funny story that I went and stole the ring from her parents' house.
turns.zh: 离婚率最低的那对夫妇，婚礼花费不到一千美元。我太太可以讲一个趣事：我当初是从她父母家把戒指'偷'出来的。

turns.en: That was pretty funny. Welcome to episode 426 of the Rashed Reminder podcast. We are hosted by me, Benjamin Felix, Dan Bordelotti, and Ben Wilson, all of PWL Capital.
turns.zh: 那确实挺好笑。欢迎收听 Rational Reminder 播客第 426 期。主持人是我 Benjamin Felix，还有 Dan Bortolotti 和 Ben Whitmore，我们都来自 PWL Capital。

turns.en: Be back with you. Yeah. Looking forward to it. Could be back. So we're going to jump right into our main topic here, which is the finances of marriage or the personal finances of marriage, or maybe the interpersonal finances of marriage, I don't know.
turns.zh: （广告回来）我们继续。是啊，很期待。好，我们直接进入本期主题——婚姻的财务，或者说是婚姻中的个人理财，又或者是婚姻里 interpersonal 的财务，我也叫不准。

turns.en: There's a bunch of interesting research on this that we'll talk through and then stick around. At the end, we will put together a little after show.
turns.zh: 这方面有一堆有趣的研究，我们会一条条聊过去。然后请留下来，最后我们会做一个小番外（after show）。

turns.en: Some comments in the Rashed Reminder community recently suggested that people miss the chatter. I guess we used to do more of. We'll have to do more of it.
turns.zh: 最近 Rational Reminder 社群里有些评论说，大家怀念我们以前的闲聊，我想我们以前确实聊得更多。以后我们得再来点。

turns.en: I think so. I think that's the message. Okay, so who are you married? I'll be interested in your commentary, Dan and Ben, as we go through this because we are all married people.
turns.zh: 我也这么觉得，我想这就是大家的心声。好，你们都结婚了吗？Dan、Ben，一会儿我很好奇你们的评论，因为我们都是已婚人士。

turns.en: How long have you been married? I'm actually 15 years on Thursday and a rooster is this week. I'm 32 this year. Man, yeah. Okay. So I've been married 12 years, which I thought was a long time, but definitely interested in your input as we go even more so.
turns.zh: 结婚多久了？其实我下周四就满 15 年了，就在这周。我今年 32 岁。嗯，不错。我结婚 12 年了，本来觉得挺长，但听你们两位讲，我会更感兴趣。

turns.en: Who you marry is obviously one of the most impactful decisions of your life, both financially and of course, otherwise. But I think a lot of couples let their finances be an afterthought or their financial compatibility be an afterthought.
turns.zh: 和谁结婚显然是你人生中最有影响力的决定之一，不仅在财务上，当然也在其他方面。但我觉得很多夫妻让财务问题——或者说财务兼容性——成了事后才考虑的附属品。

turns.en: But the reality is that who you decide to marry and how you structure your finances and make decisions together compounds across every major life decision that you make going forward.
turns.zh: 但现实是，你选择和谁结婚、你们如何搭建财务结构、如何做共同决策，会在你今后每一个重大人生决定上产生复利效应。

turns.en: I don't think anybody would disagree with this statement. If you mess up the marriage thing, the costs can be pretty devastating, both financially, divorce can be very expensive, but obviously otherwise as well, emotionally and psychologically and all that stuff.
turns.zh: 我想没人会反对这句话。如果婚姻这件事搞砸了，代价可能是毁灭性的：离婚在财务上可能非常昂贵，但在情感、心理等各种层面同样如此。

turns.en: I'm not a marriage counselor or an expert in marriage. You guys are more so than I am with your more years of experience, I guess. But there is a ton of research on this topic, which is what we're going to be speaking to.
turns.zh: 我不是婚姻咨询师，也不是婚姻方面的专家——论经验，你们两位年限更长，应该比我资深。但这个主题确实有大量研究，正是我们要聊的。

turns.en: We've also got, and again, this is where I'll be interested in your guys thoughts as we go through this than have been. We deal with a lot of clients, a lot of Canadian households and a lot of households are couples.
turns.zh: 还有一点——这也是我期待你们想法的地方——我们日常服务大量客户、大量加拿大家庭，而很多家庭都是夫妻。

turns.en: They're married. And then the other unfortunate thing that we see in our role as financial advisors is people do get divorced. We get a pretty good cross-section of couples and finances just through our professional work.
turns.zh: 是已婚夫妻。而且作为财务顾问，我们看到的另一个不幸现实是：人们确实会离婚。通过专业工作，我们对夫妻及其财务状况有一个相当有代表性的横截面。

turns.en: And the last thing I'll say as a setup for the topic is that the Harvard study of adult development, which is one of the longest running studies of human happiness, a psychiatrist wrote a book based on those data.
turns.zh: 最后一点铺垫：哈佛成人发展研究（Harvard Study of Adult Development），是追踪人类幸福最久的大型研究之一，一位精神病学家基于那些数据写了一本书。

turns.en: And one of the six factors of a healthy aging, this psychiatrist found was a stable marriage. I think it's something that's really worth getting right and doing well.
turns.zh: 他归纳的健康老龄化的六个要素之一，就是稳定的婚姻。我觉得这是非常值得认真对待、努力做好的事。

turns.en: And there's a bunch of research on how to do that, which is what we're going to talk about. Any comments before I keep going? I think it's a super interesting topic and obviously finances is a part of what you interact with in a marriage.
turns.zh: 关于怎么做好它有很多研究，这正是我们要聊的。我继续之前，你们有什么想说的吗？我觉得这个主题特别有意思，而财务显然是婚姻中你们要面对的一部分。

turns.en: It's usually not a primary consideration, but it's probably at least a secondary consideration when you're in the courting, dating phase. You notice things.
turns.zh: 它通常不是首要考量，但在追求、约会阶段，它至少是个次要考量——你会注意到一些事情。

turns.en: It may not be the reason you go forward or stop a relationship, but it's definitely something that people notice and especially if you got together young, it may be hard to recognize what impact they might have over a long term.
turns.zh: 它可能不是你继续或结束一段关系的原因，但人们确实会注意到。尤其是如果你们年轻时在一起，很难意识到对方在长期里会有多大影响。

turns.en: So it's important to think about that, especially if you're not at that stage yet or if you've been burned once through a divorce, finances might have been one of the reasons that led to divorce and it probably changes your perspective on how to approach a future relationship.
turns.zh: 所以早点想这个很重要，尤其如果你还没到那个阶段；或者如果你曾在离婚里受过伤——财务可能正是导致离婚的原因之一——那它多半会改变你面对下一段关系的心态。

turns.en: I think that's it. Most people make this decision when they're quite young, unless it's a second marriage, but usually when you are deciding on a partner that you want to spend your life with, you're probably not at the same financial position then that you will be at some point in the future and it's often difficult to really know what you're getting yourself into on that.
turns.zh: 我觉得大多数人做这个决定时都相当年轻，除非是第二次婚姻。通常当你选定想共度一生的伴侣时，你当时的财务状况和未来某个时点的状态多半不一样，而且往往很难真正清楚自己将踏入什么。

turns.en: As a couple, you evolve over time in the same way. In other words, you don't become more different and more extreme over time that you learn together your financial situation changes together at the same pace and you can both update your expectations along the way.
turns.zh: 作为夫妻，你们也会一起随时间演变。换句话说，你们不会越变越不同、越变越极端，而是一起学习、以同样的步调一起让财务状况变化，并且一起更新彼此的预期。

turns.en: Some of the research does speak to that. The effect that joint finances can have on the relationship that a couple has with money as opposed to if they have separate finances and I think some of that's what you mentioned if one person's financial situation is changing and they have separate finances, that can become pretty difficult for a couple to manage together.
turns.zh: 确实有些研究说到这一点——共同管理财务与分开管理财务，对夫妻金钱关系的影响不同。我想你刚才也提到：如果一方的财务状况在变，而两人财务分开，那对夫妻共同经营会相当困难。

turns.en: Just on people changing over time, some of the research that we'll talk about does show that there is a pretty stable characteristic in terms of your propensity to spend, which we'll also talk about.
turns.zh: 就人会随时间改变这点而言，我们接下来要讲的一些研究显示，你的消费倾向（propensity to spend）其实是一个相当稳定的特质，这个我们也会聊到。

turns.en: Marriage is obviously a big commitment. This commitment you make emotionally, but it also changes the legal nature of your relationship. It comes with real legal obligations and liabilities.
turns.zh: 婚姻显然是个大承诺。这是情感上的承诺，但它也改变了你们关系的法律性质，伴随着实实在在的法律义务和责任。

turns.en: Now, I know obligations and liabilities don't sound very romantic, but I think that's the reality of marriage. It's as much about love as it is about commitment and the law tends to support that commitment that you say you're wanting to make.
turns.zh: 我知道'义务'和'责任'听起来不怎么浪漫，但我觉得这就是婚姻的现实：它既关乎爱，也关乎承诺，而法律倾向于支持你宣称要许下的那个承诺。

turns.en: Entering into a marriage ends up being this really big financial decision. You're sharing your life with somebody, but you're also sort of incurring these costs if you want to walk away from the marriage in the future.
turns.zh: 进入婚姻最终是一个非常大的财务决定。你和一个人共享人生，但如果你将来想退出这段婚姻，某种程度上你就承担了这些成本。

turns.en: We're going to walk through what the research says about the finances of marriage across five different questions that shape how our relationships connect to our finances.
turns.zh: 我们会围绕五个不同的问题，梳理研究对婚姻财务的结论，这些问题决定了亲密关系如何与财务交织。

turns.en: Choosing who to marry, as Ben you mentioned, obviously goes way beyond finances, but I think it's worth understanding what the evidence says about who is compatible long-term in terms of their financial behaviors.
turns.zh: 第一个，选择谁结婚。正如 Ben 所说，这当然远超财务范畴，但我认为值得了解：从长期看，哪些人的财务行为在兼容性上更有证据支持。

turns.en: This is research we've talked about in the past. We've actually had Scott Rick, one of the co-authors on the podcast, I don't remember what episode that was, but this is based on a 2008 paper that conceptualized a scale of spending behavior from tight wads to spend a thrift.
turns.zh: 这是我们以前聊过的研究，我们还请过 Scott Rick——论文合著者之一——来做客节目，我记不清是哪一期了。这基于 2008 年的一篇论文，他们把消费行为概念化为一个从'抠门者'（tightwad）到'挥霍者'（spendthrift）的量表。

turns.en: The key difference between those two profiles, those two ends of the spectrum or the scale, is how they experience what the authors call an anticipatory pain of pain.
turns.zh: 这两端画像的关键区别，在于他们如何体验作者所说的'支付预期之痛'（anticipatory pain of pay）。

turns.en: That's an immediate emotional response felt at the moment of purchase rather than a rational calculation about future consequences or payoffs.
turns.zh: 那是在购买瞬间感受到的即时情绪反应，而不是对未来后果或回报的理性计算。

turns.en: The difference is that tight wads feel that pain of spending money too acutely and they spend less than they would ideally like to. That's the key there is that not that they're frugal, which I'll touch on in a second, but they're spending less than they would prefer to be spending.
turns.zh: 区别在于：抠门者对花钱之痛的感受过于强烈，他们花得比自己理想中想花的更少。关键在这里——不是节俭（frugal），我马上会讲——而是花得低于他们自己希望的量。

turns.en: They look at like their ideal version of themselves, they'll be whatever, I don't know, going out to dinner more often, they're buying things for people or whatever it might be, but they are spending less than that because it hurts them to spend.
turns.zh: 对照他们理想中的自己——比如多出去吃几顿晚饭、给别人买东西，什么都行——他们就是花不到那个量，因为花钱让他们疼。

turns.en: I will mention the difference between that and being frugal, frugal is deriving pleasure from saving, being a tight wad is incurring pain from spending.
turns.zh: 我说一下它和节俭的区别：节俭是从存钱中获得乐趣；抠门是从花钱中承受痛苦。

turns.en: Then the other end of the spectrum, spend thrifts, they tend to feel too little anticipatory pain when spending and they end up spending more than they would ideally like to.
turns.zh: 光谱另一端的挥霍者，花钱时感受到的预期之痛太少，结果花得比自己理想中想花的更多。

turns.en: The scale is really measured as that gap between your ideal self and where your behavior actually places you. They do persist over time, just in terms of can people change over time.
turns.zh: 这个量表衡量的其实就是理想自我与实际行为之间的落差。这些倾向确实会随时间持续存在——就人能否随时间改变而言。

turns.en: There is research in psychology that shows that if you're aware of your own behavioral patterns that can help you to change them. So even if these are persistent traits over time, if you know you're a tight wad or you know you're a spend thrift, I think you're in a better position to moderate that.
turns.zh: 心理学研究表明，如果你意识到自己的行为模式，就能帮助你改变它。所以即使这些是持久的特质，如果你知道自己是抠门者或挥霍者，我认为你就更有条件把它往中间调。

turns.en: So it's something that's worth understanding about yourself, potential partner, I think it's kind of a weird dinner conversation to have, but maybe worthwhile when you're making that decision.
turns.zh: 所以这值得对自己、对潜在伴侣有个了解。我猜这是个有点怪的饭桌话题，但也许在做决定时值得一聊。

turns.en: So ask your partner if they're a tight wad or a spend thrift and see how they respond. And there's a quiz. We'll post a link to it in the episode notes.
turns.zh: 所以问问你的伴侣是抠门者还是挥霍者，看他们怎么反应。有个测评问卷，我们会在节目笔记里放链接。

turns.en: Scott Rick and his co-authors, when they wrote this paper back in 2008, I think, they came up with this scale. How do you measure tight wadism or being a spend thrift?
turns.zh: Scott Rick 和他的合著者在 2008 年写这篇论文的时候，琢磨了怎么测量'抠门'或'挥霍'。

turns.en: And they come up with this three-question scale, so you answer the questions, you get a score and it tells you what your profile is. I did this when I went on the Diary of a CO podcast.
turns.zh: 他们想出了一个三问题的量表：你回答问题，得到一个分数，它告诉你属于哪一类。我在上 Diary of a CEO 播客的时候就做过。

turns.en: I did this quiz with Stephen as we were recording and at that time I was unconflected. I took it again today and this time I was a tight wad just barely one point over.
turns.zh: 我和 Stephen 录节目的时候做了这个测评，当时我是'无冲突型'（unconflicted）。今天我又做了一遍，这次成了抠门者，刚好超出一分。

turns.en: What's changed? I don't know. I don't remember. I don't know what I answered differently or I think I was right on the edge as maybe a 10 last time I took it and I was an 11 this time.
turns.zh: 什么变了？我不知道，也不记得了，也许我答案哪里变了。我上次大概正好在边缘，是 10 分，这次是 11 分。

turns.en: So I'm very close to being an unconflected tight wad. I'm just over the edge. I took it today too, sort of my wife and we're both at the low end of the unconflected consumer.
turns.zh: 所以我很接近'无冲突型偏抠门'，就刚过线。我今天也跟我太太一起做了，我们俩都在'无冲突型'的偏低端。

turns.en: I was 12, she was 13 and tight wad is 11 and below. So I came in at 16, which is unconflected, but I guess closer to the high end, which surprised me a little bit.
turns.zh: 我是 12 分，她是 13 分，而 11 分及以下算抠门者。我是 16 分，属于无冲突型，但偏高端，这多少让我有点意外。

turns.en: But what's interesting about this whole definition is it doesn't have anything to do with the amount of money you spend in any objective way.
turns.zh: 但这个定义最有意思的一点是：它和你花多少钱完全无关，没有任何客观衡量。

turns.en: In other words, you could be very wealthy and be a tight wad and you could be living on the edge of bankruptcy and be a spendthrift. It has nothing to do with the amount of money that in other words, from the outside, I don't think people would be able to identify spendthrifts and tight wads because it really comes down to how faithful you think you are being to yourself.
turns.zh: 也就是说，你可能非常有钱却是个抠门者，也可能在破产边缘却是个挥霍者，与金额无关。换言之，从外部看，我觉得别人无法识别谁是挥霍者、谁是抠门者，因为这归根结底在于你觉得自己在多大程度上忠于自己。

turns.en: The tight wad is someone who deep down wishes they could spend more but can't bring themselves to, which is not the same thing as somebody who doesn't get any value from spending.
turns.zh: 抠门者是内心深处想多花却下不了手的人，这和花钱得不到任何价值的人不是一回事。

turns.en: So I think that's an important distinction to make. I think that's very important. It's relative to your ability or your means to spend. It's like I've seen clients or other people, friends that have a lot of wealth and they're under spending relative to the plan.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这个区分很重要，非常重要。它是相对于你的支付能力和财力而言的。我见过客户或朋友很有钱，但他们的消费远低于自己的计划。

turns.en: We've gone through with clients and looked at you could spend X amount multiples more than what they're currently spending and they're like, I have no idea what I could spend money on and whether they're considered a tight wad or not would differ depending on the perception of whoever's looking at them.
turns.zh: 我们和客户一起梳理过：你们其实可以花掉目前开支的好几倍，他们却说'我根本不知道钱还能花在哪'。至于是不算抠门者，取决于旁观者怎么 perception。

turns.en: Someone from the outside sees a friend spending 10, 12,000 a month sees like they're a spendthrift but on their balance sheet, they're spending at way lower capacity of where they could possibly spend versus other clients spend way beyond the means or friends or peers in your circles and you can notice a difference there.
turns.zh: 外人看一个每月花一万、一万二千美元的朋友，会觉得是挥霍者；但对照资产负债表，他们离自己可能的消费上限还远得很。也有客户、朋友、圈子里的人花得远超承受能力，你能看出差别。

turns.en: There's people who can't figure out what to spend money on. I think that's a separate issue. The tight wad is someone who they wish they could spend more money and they just can't bring themselves to do it and I think we do see that too.
turns.zh: 有人是不知道怎么花钱——我觉得那是另一回事。抠门者是希望能多花却就是下不了手的人，我觉得我们也确实见过这种。

turns.en: For sure. I know that's something that some clients get a lot of value from the perspective of the service that PWL provides where if we're able to encourage them and tell them, yes, it's really okay for you to do this, I think that can help reduce some of the pain that they get from spending.
turns.zh: 对。我知道有些客户特别从 PWL 提供的服务价值里获益：如果我们能鼓励他们、告诉他们'你真的可以这样花'，我想这能减轻他们花钱时的痛苦。

turns.en: Something we have not done that would be interesting is getting people to take the tight wad spendthrift scale and then just be able to show them, listen, this is how you are classified as a spender.
turns.zh: 我们还没做、但可能有趣的一件事是：让大家做这个'抠门—挥霍'量表，然后告诉他们——看，你是这样分类的。

turns.en: Let's think about how to address that because some of the research and psychology does suggest that if you just like name an issue that you're having and have a framework to think about it, that can help you actually move away from the behavior that you're not happy about.
turns.zh: 我们再想想怎么应对。心理学研究确实表明，只要给困扰你的问题命名、建立一个思考框架，就能帮你偏离你自己不满意的那个行为。

turns.en: That's an interesting point because we spend a lot of time giving risk questionnaires and things like that, which is important, but I think especially once you get to the drawdown stage, just as important as it is to understand whether you're a conservative, balanced or aggressive investor is what kind of spender you are.
turns.zh: 这是很有意思的一点。我们花很多时间做风险问卷这类东西，这当然重要；但我认为，尤其到了支取期（drawdown），了解自己是保守型、平衡型还是进取型投资者，和了解你是哪种类型的消费者同样重要。

turns.en: The point is not that you have the means to spend or not. It's about how faithful you are to your own deep desire. A tight wad is not someone who doesn't get a lot of pleasure from spending.
turns.zh: 重点不是你有没有消费能力。关键在于你有多大程度上忠于自己内心深处的渴望。抠门者不是花钱得不到多少乐趣的人——

turns.en: It's someone who deep down wishes they could get more pleasure from spending than they're actually getting and that's an important distinction.
turns.zh: 而是内心希望能比现在获得更多花钱乐趣的人——这是个重要区分。

turns.en: Let's say for example, you had the capacity to spend 300 grand a year because you were very wealthy, but you were perfectly and utterly content with yourself spending half that.
turns.zh: 举个例子：假设你有能力一年花 30 万加元，因为非常有钱，但你花一半就对自己完全、彻底地满意。

turns.en: You're not a tight wad, you're probably an unconflected consumer unless you're spending as much as you possibly can, then you have some sort of tight wad aspect to you.
turns.zh: 那你就不是抠门者，多半是无冲突型——除非你把能花的都花光了，那你身上倒是有点抠门者的成分。

turns.en: Really, I think it comes down to what you enjoy and what gives you pain. I think for some people, spending money just hurts so much that they don't derive any enjoyment from things that other people would absolutely derive enjoyment from.
turns.zh: 我觉得归根结底在于你喜欢什么、什么让你痛苦。对一些人来说，花钱实在太痛了，别人乐在其中的事，他们完全体会不到乐趣。

turns.en: Another probably ties into the happiness and positive psychology literature and being able to tell people like, listen, spending money on this stuff tends to make people feel really good.
turns.zh: 这也大概连着幸福与积极心理学的研究——你可以告诉客户：在这些事上花钱，人们普遍会感觉很好，我们要不要试一下？

turns.en: Why don't we try it? I'm going to read through the questions real quick because we said we're going to link the quiz, which we will do, but it's a podcast so people are listening, not sitting at their computers waiting to take a quiz.
turns.zh: 我把题目快速念一遍，因为我们说了会放测评链接——会放的——但这是播客，大家在听，不会坐在电脑前等着做题。

turns.en: Some people have trouble limiting their spending. They often spend money, for example, on clothes, meals, vacations when they would do better not to.
turns.zh: '有些人管不住自己的开支，常常在衣服、餐饮、度假上花钱，而其实不花更好。'

turns.en: Other people have trouble spending money. That's because spending money makes them anxious. They often don't spend money on things they should spend it on.
turns.zh: '另一些人则难以花钱，因为花钱让他们焦虑，他们常常在该花钱的事上不舍得花。'

turns.en: How well does the first description fit you? That is, do you have trouble limiting your spending? And then there's answers from never to always.
turns.zh: '第一个描述与你相符的程度——即你是否管不住开支？'答案选项从'从不'到'总是'。

turns.en: How well does the second description fit you? That is, do you have trouble spending money? And again, from never to always. Following is a scenario describing the behavior of two shoppers.
turns.zh: '第二个描述与你相符的程度——即你是否难以花钱？'同样从'从不'到'总是'。'下面是一段情景，描述两位购物者的行为。'

turns.en: After reading about each shopper, please answer the question that follows. Person A is accompanying a good friend who is on a shopping spree at a local mall.
turns.zh: '读完每位购物者的描述后，请回答后面的问题。A 正陪同一位好友在当地商场大采购。走进一家大型百货商店时，A 看到店里只限一天、全场降价 10% 到 60% 的促销。'

turns.en: When they enter a large department store, Person A sees that the store has a one day only sale where everything is priced 10 to 60% off. Person A realizes they don't need anything, yet can't resist and end up spending almost $100 on stuff.
turns.zh: 'A 意识到自己并不需要任何东西，却没能忍住，最后花了将近 100 美元买东西。'

turns.en: Person B is accompanying a good friend who is on a shopping spree at a local mall. When they enter a large department store, Person B sees that the store has a one day only sale where everything is priced 10 to 60% off.
turns.zh: 'B 正陪同一位好友在当地商场大采购。走进一家大型百货商店时，B 看到店里只限一天、全场降价 10% 到 60% 的促销。'

turns.en: Person B figures they can get great deals on many items that they need yet. The thought of spending money keeps them from buying stuff. In terms of your own behavior, who are you more similar to Person A or Person B?
turns.zh: 'B 觉得自己可以在很多需要的东西上捡到大便宜，但一想到花钱就让他买不下去。就你自己的行为而言，你更像 A 还是 B？'

turns.en: And then the last question, you just indicate on a scale. So they say, consider which of the following descriptions fits you better. I find it difficult to spend money or I have difficulty controlling my spending.
turns.zh: '最后一题只需在量表上选。以下哪个描述更适合你：我难以花钱，还是我难以控制消费？'

turns.en: And you select the number from 1 to 11 where 1 is difficult to spend money and 11 is difficulty controlling spending and then it spits out a score.
turns.zh: '从 1 到 11 选一个数：1 是难以花钱，11 是难以控制消费，然后系统给出你的得分。'

turns.en: Pretty simple. Hopefully people will take it and let us know where they land. My hunch based on my many years of interactions with folks listening to our podcast is that there's going to be a whole lot of tight wads in there.
turns.zh: 很简单。希望大家测完告诉我们自己落在哪。凭我和听众多年打交道的直觉，我猜'抠门者'会占相当大比例。

turns.en: But we'll see. It's interesting because I tend to be a big saver and I thought I was going to be more of a tight wad and ended up in the unconflected consumer.
turns.zh: 不过走着看。有意思的是，我平时很爱存钱，本以为自己会更偏抠门者，结果落在了无冲突型。

turns.en: That's healthier. Like you can be disciplined. I agree. And unconflected. For sure. That to be a more common answer, but that's just speculation because most people I've talked to are happy with what they're spending, whether it's perceived as spending too much or too little.
turns.zh: 那更健康。你可以有纪律性。同意。而且是'无冲突型'。对。那可能才是更常见的答案——不过这纯属猜测，因为我接触的多数人对自己的消费挺满意，无论别人觉得花多了还是花少了。

turns.en: I have not experienced in conversation as much where they wish they could spend more, but they're not or the opposite. I don't know if you guys have seen something different in your interactions.
turns.zh: 我倒很少在对话中遇到那种'想多花却做不到'或者反过来的人。不知道你们在互动中有没有看到不一样的。

turns.en: Don't recall conversations specifically where it's like I'm not spending as much money as I wish I could spend. I haven't been in front of clients in a long time.
turns.zh: 我不记得有具体的对话说'我花的钱没有我希望的那么多'。我已经很久不在一线面对客户了。

turns.en: I've definitely had conversations where that is the case. This discussion popped up in the Rational Minor community a week ago or two weeks ago.
turns.zh: 我确实有过这样的对话。大概一两周前，这个讨论在 Rational Reminder 社群里出现过。

turns.en: And there was a whole discussion about this. It was from our myths and personal finance episode. People were discussing that, the saving that you need to save as much as you possibly can when you're young myth.
turns.zh: 当时聊了很长一串，出自我们的'个人理财神话'那期。大家在讨论'年轻时有多少存多少'这个神话。

turns.en: That one sets people off all the time anyway. It led to this discussion about exactly what we're talking about and there were a whole bunch of people in there telling stories about family members or clients who have been in this exact situation where they had a desire to buy stuff or go on trips or do whatever, but they just couldn't bring themselves to spend the money even though they knew they had the money there.
turns.zh: 那个观点总是能激起反应，进而聊到正是我们今天说的内容。帖子里一堆人讲家人或客户的经历，一模一样的处境：想买、想旅行、想做点什么，却就是花不出去，明明知道钱就在那儿。

turns.en: One person gave their own story about how they're retired and they're going on a trip. I think it was to Europe. They have the means to do so.
turns.zh: 有一位讲了自己的故事：已经退休，要出去旅行，好像是去欧洲，钱完全够。

turns.en: They wanted to upgrade their seats to the life-flat business class seats and their spouse just wouldn't do it. They can afford it. It's no problem.
turns.zh: 他们想把座位升级成全平躺（lie-flat）商务舱，但他的配偶就是不愿意。明明负担得起，完全没问题。

turns.en: Whatever. They can't bring themselves to spend the money. That's a good example. Yeah. Spending on things that don't feel reasonable based on your upbringing, that's much more common for someone that's gotten to a level of wealth where spending $6,000 on a flight to Europe, for example, seems crazy if you grew up middle class or lower middle class, but if you're wealthy now, the amount of spending is irrelevant to your current situation.
turns.zh: 反正就是舍不得花那笔钱。这个例子很好。对，花那种在你成长环境看来'不合理'的钱，更常见：如果你的成长环境是中产或中产偏下，即使现在富裕了，花 6,000 美元买一张去欧洲的机票也像疯了——但金额和你现在的处境已经无关了。

turns.en: That is much more common, I found. I think that's a good point. I wonder how much of it relates to how conscious you are of status, and I think it can cut both ways.
turns.zh: 我觉得那种更常见，说得很好。我在想这和你在多大程度上在意身份地位（status）有关，而且我觉得这东西可以往两个方向走。

turns.en: I think there are some people who like to use your business class life-flat seats. I think there might be some people who would feel quite proud being in that section of the plane and feeling like I'm signaling to other people how wealthy or how successful I am, and other people who might take the opposite, who feel like, I don't know, it feels like showing off to me.
turns.zh: 我想有些人坐全平躺商务舱会挺自豪，觉得我在向别人展示自己多有财力、多成功；另一些人可能正好相反，觉得那像是在炫耀。

turns.en: Those people could both have the same means to spend. Again, it comes down to the kind of tight-wad spin-thrift inclination is about how your spending relates to your own identity, who you think you are, how you want your spending to appear to other people.
turns.zh: 这两类人可能有同样的消费能力。说到底，'抠门—挥霍'的倾向关乎你的消费和你认同的自我：你觉得自己是谁、你希望自己的消费在别人眼中是什么样子。

turns.en: If that's important to you at all, and I think the happiest people are the ones who don't care what other people think about what they spend their money on.
turns.zh: 如果这点对你重要的话——我觉得最幸福的人，是那些根本不在乎别人怎么看自己花钱的人。

turns.en: I'm not interested in other people judging me favorably or unfavorably on what I spend. I think if that's your attitude, probably quite a bit more content.
turns.zh: 我不希望别人因为我的花钱方式对我有好评或差评。如果你是这种心态，大概率会知足得多。

turns.en: That shows up a ton in the happiness literature. The effects of social comparison are unequivocally horrific for happiness. We're getting a little bit sidetracked here, which is fine, but back to how this relates to marriage.
turns.zh: 幸福研究里大量显示这一点：社会比较对幸福的负面影响是确定无疑的糟糕。我们有点跑题了，没关系——回到婚姻。

turns.en: We've got these tight-wads and we've got these spin-thrifts. The evidence here gets quite interesting. Tight-wads and spin-thrifts are more likely to marry each other than to marry a tight-wad or another spin-thrift.
turns.zh: 这里有抠门者，也有挥霍者。证据部分开始有意思了：抠门者和挥霍者更容易与对方结婚，而不是与同类人结婚。

turns.en: If you're a tight-wad, you're more likely to marry a spin-thrift, is what their research showed, at least in the sample that they had studied there.
turns.zh: 也就是说，如果你是抠门者，你更可能找一个挥霍者结婚——至少在他们的研究样本里是这样。

turns.en: It's kind of like we hear opposites attract, but I think the findings may be a little bit counterintuitive when you consider that in reality, people do tend to find spouses who share some characteristics, which without seeing the research, you might expect that to include spending tendencies, but the research shows the opposite, which I guess is why it was an interesting finding.
turns.zh: 有点像我们常说的'异性相吸'。但这个发现其实有点反直觉：现实中人们通常还是会找有共同特质的人做配偶——不论文献的话，你会以为消费倾向也算，但研究恰恰相反，所以这才是有趣的发现。

turns.en: They do suggest a couple of reasons for the disconnect or for why opposites attract. People tend to have poor introspective awareness of what they'll actually find attractive when encountering real potential partners, and when tight-wads and spin-thrifts encounter similar behaviors to their own in others, it reminds them of that negative behavior, quality in themselves.
turns.zh: 他们给了两个解释。一是，人们在遇到真实的潜在伴侣时，其实并不清楚自己会被什么吸引；二是，当抠门者看到别人的抠门、挥霍者看到别人的挥霍，那会让他们想起自己身上那个负面特质。

turns.en: The result is what the authors describe as fatal fiscal attractions, where someone who doesn't share your same shortcomings from a spending perspective is initially exciting and appealing to you for that reason, but then the reason that this is important is what the study then goes on to show is that that excitement is transitory, and then later on tight-wads and spin-thrifts that marry one another tend to experience more frequent
turns.zh: 结果就是作者所说的'致命的财务吸引'（fatal fiscal attraction）——一个和你有不同消费缺点的人，一开始让你兴奋、被吸引。重要的是，研究接下来表明这种兴奋是短暂的，

turns.en: conflicts over money and diminished marital well-being. The more they differ on the scale, so the more extreme you are on one end or the other, the more likely you are to have marital conflict.
turns.zh: 之后，抠门者与挥霍者结成的婚姻往往有更频繁的钱的冲突，婚姻幸福感也更低。两个人在量表上差得越远——你在一端越极端——婚姻冲突越可能多。

turns.en: They find that that remains true even when debt and savings in the household are controlled for. That doesn't mean that two people who have different spending profiles will be dissatisfied with their marriage.
turns.zh: 在控制了家庭的债务和储蓄之后，这个结论依然成立。但这并不意味着消费画像不同的两个人就一定对婚姻不满意。

turns.en: It also doesn't mean that you should marry some of those who are going to mirror your own financial behavior, but I think it is useful to have that framework for better understanding yourself and your spouse and your respective emotions around spending money, and I do think having that understanding, like Ben, you said, you and your wife both did the quiz.
turns.zh: 也不意味着你非得找一个在财务行为上完全复制你的配偶。但我认为这个框架能帮你理解自己和配偶各自对花钱的情绪反应。像 Ben 说的，你和太太一起做了测评。

turns.en: My wife and I both did it as well, not today, but a while ago, and similarly, we were on the same page there, two people are different. The fact that they're different, what the research shows is not great, but I think understanding where each person is coming from can put you on a better footing.
turns.zh: 我太太和我也做过，不是今天，是之前，结果我们也很接近。两个人有差异，研究说这不是好消息，但理解彼此从哪里来，能让你们站得更好。

turns.en: And then, of course, if you're not married yet and you're kind of dating, this is something that you can either explicitly by telling them to do the quiz or asking them to do the quiz, or you can just try and feel out, but it's a trait worth understanding, I think, in a partner or a potential partner.
turns.zh: 当然，如果还没结婚、正在约会阶段，这要么直接让对方做测评，要么自己去感受——总之，这是伴侣或潜在伴侣身上值得了解的特质。

turns.en: As with many areas of marriage, it opens a dialogue and transparent communication is important. As you've said, whether you're opposite or the same doesn't necessarily set you up for success or failure, but having this information equips you to have conversations in a healthy way, that you can see the different perspectives and plan together, maybe you may compromise as on different big financial decisions, but you can understand the perspective of each
turns.zh: 和婚姻中的很多方面一样，重要的是打开对话、保持透明的沟通。你已经说过了：相同还是互补并不决定成败，但掌握这些信息能让你们用健康的方式沟通、看到不同视角、一起规划，在大的财务决定上彼此妥协、理解对方的立场。

turns.en: other. It makes conversations better. It's not about you're irresponsible, it's like, oh, you have a psychological tendency to behave this way.
turns.zh: 这会让对话质量不一样。重点不是'你不负责任'，而是'你有一种心理上会这样消费的模式'。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. In some cases, you could probably actually bring out the best of the other person, like a tightwad. It may help to encourage them to spend more when they want to spend, and the opposite spends for thrift may end up saving more when they feel bad about overspending.
turns.zh: 对，正是如此。有些情况下你们反而能激发对方最好的一面：比如对抠门者，鼓励他在想花的时候花；

turns.en: It could end up in a healthy relationship, balancing each other out to be a more positive experience. Yeah, you can see that kind of gift giving, for example, right?
turns.zh: 而挥霍者一方因为超支内疚时反而可能多存一点。这可能成就一种互补的健康关系，让整体体验更积极。你看送礼就是典型的例子：

turns.en: Somebody who was a tightwad would presumably be very reluctant to purchase something. Even though deep down they know they'd enjoy it, they just can't justify the expense.
turns.zh: 抠门者多半很不舍得买某样东西，尽管内心深处知道自己会喜欢，但就是没法说服自己花那笔钱。

turns.en: But if a spendthrift spouse were to purchase that for them, that probably gives both of them pleasure, because the tightwad is going to enjoy this gift, even if he or she wouldn't have bought it for themselves, and then the spouse has the pleasure of knowing that they gave a gift that made their partner happy.
turns.zh: 如果挥霍者一方替他把礼物买下来，双方都会开心：收礼的一方会享受这个礼物——即便自己绝不会买——送礼的一方也有'让伴侣快乐'的满足感。

turns.en: So I can certainly see if the compromises are good ones, that having those kind of opposite personalities can actually result in each one making the other one a little bit better or a little bit happier anyway.
turns.zh: 所以我完全能想象，如果妥协是好的，这些互补的性格反而让彼此变得更好一点、更快乐一点。

turns.en: Especially if you know where the other person's coming from. In the gift example, you can imagine a scenario where a real tightwad gets upset about having been given a gift.
turns.zh: 前提是你了解对方从哪里来。就拿送礼来说，你也能想象另一种剧情：一个真正的抠门者收到礼物反而生气，

turns.en: Especially an expensive gift. I can't believe you spent money on this. Yeah, it has to be within reason, right? But you're right. That's the compromise.
turns.zh: 尤其礼物很贵的时候：'真不敢相信你竟然花这个钱！''是啊，得在合理范围内嘛。不过你说得对，这就是妥协。'

turns.en: That's where if everyone's on the same page, and yeah, it's a super interesting strand of research and practically useful for couples. The next one is whether you should get a prenuptial agreement, which Ontario is called a marriage contract.
turns.zh: 如果大家在同一页上就好办。这确实是一个非常有趣、又对夫妻实用的研究方向。下一个问题是：要不要签婚前协议（prenup），在安大略省叫'婚姻协议'（marriage contract）。

turns.en: I'm sure it's got different names in other places, but people kind of know what the idea is there. One thing that's important to understand up front with a prenuptial or a marriage contract is that everyone has one by default when you get married based on the family law set up where you live.
turns.zh: 其他地方可能有别的名字，但意思大家明白。首先要了解的是：一结婚，根据你所在地的家庭法，每个人默认就已经有一份'协议'了。

turns.en: So you got to understand what the law says in Ontario or in Quebec, wherever you are as a starting point. And that's actually not even unique to marriage.
turns.zh: 所以你得先搞清楚安大略、魁北克或者你所在地的法律怎么规定，这是起点。而且这甚至不是婚姻独有的。

turns.en: We're kind of focused on marriage here, but that's important to understand. If you're living with someone, if you have a child with someone but aren't married, there can still be legal implications on a separation.
turns.zh: 我们今天聚焦婚姻，但这点很重要：同居、有孩子但没结婚，分开时同样可能有法律后果。

turns.en: A prenupt or a cohabitation agreement lets you pre-agree on your own set of marriage rules that are different from the standard legal prescription that your province or state or whatever has.
turns.zh: 婚前协议或同居协议，让你预先约定一套不同于你所在省、州默认法律规定的'婚姻规则'。

turns.en: Now, that's probably a good thing for most people to do. You mentioned earlier, Dan, a really good point to think on this topic specifically is that a lot of the time people are getting married, they're young and don't have a lot of financial resources.
turns.zh: Dan，你前面提到一个很好的点：很多时候人们结婚时很年轻，没有多少财务资源。

turns.en: So you wouldn't even think to do this, which makes sense. People on second marriages are probably more likely to get them, but it's something that people should be aware of the implications of and understand whether they should consider getting a prenup even if they are younger.
turns.zh: 所以根本不会想到做这个，这可以理解。二婚的人可能更倾向于签，但即便是年轻人，也应该了解其中的含义，考虑要不要签婚前协议。

turns.en: Why don't people tend to do that? Engaged couples, and this is based on one paper that found engaged couples accurately estimate the national divorce rate when they're asked, but they estimate their own chances of divorce being much lower.
turns.zh: 为什么订婚的伴侣不爱做这个？有一篇论文发现：订婚伴侣能准确估计全国的平均离婚率，

turns.en: I mean, it's the classic overconfidence, I guess, being exhibited there. So that optimism bias creates a real practical risk where couples who underestimate their likelihood of divorce may sign prenups that don't accurately reflect their post-divorce welfare needs since the agreement was designed without genuine consideration of the scenario that it's meant to govern.
turns.zh: 却大大低估自己的离婚可能性。就是经典的过度自信。这种乐观偏差带来一个实际的危险：低估离婚可能性的夫妻，签的婚前协议可能并不符合自己离婚后的福利需要——因为协议本来要应对的情形，压根没被认真考虑过。

turns.en: The other thing going on here is that law and economics research suggests that the act of requesting a prenup functions as a negative signal, showing a lack of commitment to the prospective relationship, which makes it less likely for a partner to ask for one in the first place.
turns.zh: 另一个机制是，法律经济学的研究表明：开口要求签婚前协议本身就是一个负面信号，显示对这段关系承诺不够，所以更少有人主动提出。

turns.en: So you have these two things happening. There's the optimism bias, which suppresses uptake and signaling costs deter having the conversation entirely.
turns.zh: 于是两件事同时发生：乐观偏差压低了签协议的比例，信号成本则让人们干脆不开口谈。

turns.en: And so you have these structural conditions where prenups are really underused, and when they do exist, they're potentially designed without the seriousness that the document warrants.
turns.zh: 所以从结构上看，婚前协议使用不足；而少数存在的协议，又可能配不上这份文件应有的严肃性。

turns.en: I think this concept, the way you explained it, that everybody has a default prenup, that was first explained to me and concept makes sense by Dr. Moira Summers, who's been on previous episodes and I think coming up on an episode in the near future.
turns.zh: 你刚才解释的这个概念——每个人都有默认的婚前协议——最初是 Moira Pitman 博士让我理解的，她上过我们之前的节目，我想近期还会再来一期。

turns.en: But she explained it in such a way and it kind of made a light bulb go off my head. Everybody has a default agreement set out by the law. If you're getting into this, why not create an agreement that's on your terms?
turns.zh: 她的解释让我豁然开朗：法律已经给你设定了一份默认协议，既然要进入婚姻，为什么不按自己的条件起草一份？

turns.en: But as you've said, there's this negative connotation that if you are thinking about prenup, you are thinking about the possibility of your marriage failing, which in reality, that is true.
turns.zh: 不过正如你说的，一提婚前协议就带有负面暗示——你在考虑婚姻失败的可能。而现实是，确实如此。

turns.en: You're preparing for what happens in the marriage breakdown, which is an awkward conversation. But if it does happen, it's going to be split as the law says regardless.
turns.zh: 你是在为婚姻破裂做准备，这话题很尴尬。但真发生了，该按法律怎么分还是怎么分。

turns.en: So the way Dr. Moira Summers kind of explained this was you have the opportunity to create an agreement that is drafted in a loving way that reflects your own wishes.
turns.zh: Moira Pitman 博士是这么说的：你可以用一份充满善意、反映你们真实意愿的方式来起草协议。

turns.en: You each have to get independent legal counsel. Yes. The environment doesn't appear particularly loving. So I understand the resistance, but of course, it makes a lot of sense.
turns.zh: 双方都要请独立的法律意见。是啊。这个环境看起来也不太'充满爱意'。我理解人们的抵触，但这么做当然很有道理。

turns.en: And of course, I think we all would agree they're especially important if you're coming into the marriage with very different levels of wealth.
turns.zh: 当然，我想我们都会同意：如果两个人带着很不一样的财富水平进入婚姻，那就尤其重要。

turns.en: Two young people who don't have a lot that financial assets, neither of them own a home, is it important to get one? Maybe, maybe not. But certainly if you're coming into the relationship and from very different places in net worth, one stands to be harmed a lot more in a financial sense by a breakup, for sure, makes sense to do it.
turns.zh: 两个年轻人，没什么金融资产，谁都没有房，需要签吗？可能需要，也可能不需要。但如果净资产差距悬殊，分手时财务上有一方会伤得很重，那签确实有道理。

turns.en: Yeah, that's the most obvious case. I've got some good examples of that where we've had those discussions where there is an imbalance in net worth and the way that some clients have approached it is having the large net worth spouse have their net worth kind of vest over time based on a trigger of say years or life events such as having children or if you were to pass away, maybe you get a much bigger portion, but kind of protects from the short term marriage breakdown,
turns.zh: 对，这是最典型的场景。我有好的例子：在净资产不平衡的家庭里，有些客户的做法是，让高净值一方的净资产随时间'归属'（vest）——触发条件比如年限或生育这样的生命事件，或者如果一方去世，另一方拿更大比例——它防住了短期婚姻破裂，

turns.en: but benefits for a longer term relationship. If it goes longer, the lower net worth spouse is not penalized, they still get a more representative share of the overall pie.
turns.zh: 但对长期关系给予奖励：如果婚姻走得久，低净值一方不会被亏待，最终能拿到整体蛋糕中更有代表性的份额。

turns.en: So weird to think about. Your point, Dan, is right, but then you talk to people who did get married young and one spouse ends up being very financially successful doing whatever.
turns.zh: 这么想确实有点奇怪。Dan 你说的对，但我见过一些年轻时结婚的、后来某一方在事业上非常成功。

turns.en: If they do end up getting divorced, they are often pretty unhappy. I don't know. It's tough. I don't have one. I had nothing when we got married and I didn't know I'd have a successful career at all.
turns.zh: 他们如果最后离婚，往往很不开心。我也不知道——挺难的。我结婚时几乎一无所有，当时完全不知道自己会有成功的职业。

turns.en: I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life when I got married. And here you are. And here I am. If I'm advising someone, should you get a prenup?
turns.zh: 我结婚时根本不知道自己想要什么样的人生。现在你在这儿，我也在这儿。如果要我给建议——该不该签婚前协议？

turns.en: It's tough to say. You don't want to say everybody should get a prenup. I think what you said is right, Dan. The most obvious case is if there's an obvious financial imbalance, they almost have to get one.
turns.zh: 很难说。你不能说人人都该签。我觉得 Dan 说得对：最典型的场景就是明显的财务失衡，那种几乎必须签。

turns.en: It's kind of crazy not to. If you're coming in more equally, it's a tougher conversation. Yeah. And it's tough to predict how someone's career might progress.
turns.zh: 不签反而有点疯狂。如果进来时大致平等，那就是更难的对话。是啊，而且很难预测一个人的事业会怎么发展。

turns.en: And the question of spouse partner roles, however you play, if one person decides to stay home with the children because they enjoy that or works for your family, are you in pairing their ability to earn their own income?
turns.zh: 还有夫妻角色分工的问题。如果一方决定留在家里带孩子，因为喜欢或为了家庭，你是不是就在替他们'配对'（pair）掉自己赚取收入的能力？

turns.en: Therefore, that should impact how much they get if the marriage does break down. So it gets complex pretty quick. I agree. I'm in the same scenario.
turns.zh: 那这是否应该影响离婚时他们分得的份额？所以事情很快变得复杂。我同意，我也在同样的情境里。

turns.en: I got married young and we didn't have a prenup. And because of that negative connotation, I have my own personal bias that I probably wouldn't.
turns.zh: 我年轻时结了婚，没有婚前协议。可能因为我个人也受那种负面联想的影响，我觉得我大概率也不会签。

turns.en: But the same thing, when talking to someone, I would advise them to seriously consider a prenupial agreement so that they can decide the path that makes sense for them as a couple.
turns.zh: 但同样，如果给别人建议，我会让他们认真考虑婚前协议，让他们自己决定适合夫妻双方的路径。

turns.en: I think that's where it's interesting that with this document in place, you can deliberately design your financial arrangements to reflect what makes sense for you.
turns.zh: 我觉得这才是这份文件的有趣之处：有它在，你可以有意识地设计符合自己情况的财务安排。

turns.en: If you're getting married, there is a default based on the law where you live. And so you got to know kind of baseline, what does that mean?
turns.zh: 只要结婚，你所在地就有法律默认的设定。你得先了解基线是什么意思。

turns.en: And then if that arrangement does not make sense for you, you can draft your own version of it. And you can get creative then, like you mentioned, we've seen some people get pretty creative in terms of how they want to divide assets in a hypothetical separation over time and triggered by different life events that you can do all kinds of stuff if you're doing it yourself.
turns.zh: 如果那个默认安排不适合你们，你可以自己起草一版，也可以很有创意——如我们说的——我见过一些人在假想分离中按时间、按生命事件触发来分配资产的，自己设计什么都能做。

turns.en: But I think it does have to start with an honest conversation about property and savings and income, future income, and what each person would need to be financially secure if the relationship were to end, taking a very cold and rational approach to something that is not a very cold and rational thing, which is, I think, why it's hard.
turns.zh: 但我认为得从一场诚实的对话开始：聊财产、储蓄、收入、未来的收入，如果关系结束，各自需要什么才能财务安全。对一个并不冷静理性的事情，采取一个非常冷静理性的做法——我想这正是困难所在。

turns.en: I think sometimes even having that conversation helps. I've seen people that have gone through the exercise and not formally set up the prenup, but it's helped them conceptualize, okay, something does happen.
turns.zh: 我觉得有时候光是那场对话就有帮助。我见过一些人做了这个练习，最后没有正式签婚前协议，但它帮他们理清了：如果真发生什么，我能不能接受默认的结果。

turns.en: We've discussed this and I'm okay with the default outcome or not. All right. Next one I have is, how much should you spend on an engagement ring, wedding, and honeymoon?
turns.zh: 好。下一个：订婚戒指、婚礼、蜜月，到底该花多少？

turns.en: Kind of following the arc of a marriage, choosing a partner, prenup, and wedding. There's a common perception that cheaping out on an engagement ring signals a lack of commitment or care from the proposing member of a couple, whereas prenup's act is a negative signal, a bigger ring often acts as a positive signal and an expression of love and affection.
turns.zh: 有一种普遍观感：在订婚戒指上省钱，暗示求婚的一方缺乏承诺或用心；而婚前协议是负面信号，更大的戒指则常常是正面信号、是爱意的表达。

turns.en: There are many drivers of this signaling, most notably, and I remember learning about this when I was doing my MBA as just like such a crazy marketing case, advertising from jewelry companies or diamond companies in this case, like De Beers, who first pushed the two-month salary spending standard on an engagement ring, ads like that link the price of the ring to the permanence of the marriage.
turns.zh: 这种信号背后有很多推手。最典型的——我记得读 MBA 时学过，真是个惊人的营销案例——是珠宝公司的广告，这里是钻石公司。De Beers 最早推广了'订婚戒指花两个月工资'的消费标准，这类广告把戒指的价格和婚姻的长久绑在一起。

turns.en: I remember seeing ads, the diamond is forever. When I was a kid, I haven't seen those in a long time. Brilliant marketing campaigns. Yeah. I mean, they created a market, I think, for diamonds, which is why it was such a crazy case.
turns.zh: 我小时候看过'A Diamond is Forever'的广告，已经很多年没见过了。了不起的营销。可以说他们创造了一个钻石市场，所以它才这么像个疯狂案例。

turns.en: It's a pre-tax salary. I think it's gross. I didn't look into it. I think it's gross, too, but it's funny, though, how supposed societal conventions come.
turns.zh: 那是按税前工资算吧？我想是税前毛收入，我没细查。不过所谓社会规范是怎么来的，挺有意思。

turns.en: It was a diamond company who convinced a bunch of guys that they should spend two-month salary on an engagement ring. Look, whether that's appropriate or not, not for me to say.
turns.zh: 是一家钻石公司说服了一大群男人：订婚戒指应该花两个月工资。这标准合不合适，轮不到我说。

turns.en: I just think it's also not for De Beers to say. It's bizarre how that has entered into the consciousness. Good on them. People still do it. They still blast money on engagement rings.
turns.zh: 我也觉得轮不到 De Beers 来说。它竟然进入了大众意识，真是奇怪。人家也真厉害。人们现在还在这么干，还在猛砸钱买订婚戒指。

turns.en: Honestly, two months seems low on. I've heard like three or six months. Inflation. Yeah, I certainly know of ones that were more than that, yeah, for sure.
turns.zh: 说实话，两个月现在都显得低了，我听说三个月、六个月的。通胀嘛。对，我肯定见过花得更多的。

turns.en: That's the diamonds. The interesting thing is it's not limited to the ring. I mean, we all kind of know this. There's a similar perception around the wedding itself.
turns.zh: 说回钻石。有意思的是，这种心态不止在戒指上。大家其实都知道，婚礼本身也有类似的观感。

turns.en: I've seen, separate from PWL stuff, just in my personal life, I've seen some wild weddings that I've been invited to or attended. It's just like, man, it's crazy what people will spend on a wedding.
turns.zh: 我在 PWL 业务之外，纯个人生活里，就见过一些夸张的婚礼——收到邀请或出席的。人们真敢在婚礼上花钱，太疯狂了。

turns.en: There's a 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy that found that consumers routinely attach elevated importance to wedding products that allows them to excuse excess wedding spending compared to other categories on the basis that it's a once-in-a-lifetime event that requires once-in-a-lifetime spending.
turns.zh: 2021 年 Journal of Consumer Policy 上有一篇论文发现，消费者系统性地赋予婚礼商品超高的重要性，

turns.en: What that's resulted in is a two-tiered retail market for products. We've heard about this. CBC has covered this. It's a real thing where wedding items are marked up from their regular non-wedding counterparts.
turns.zh: 从而用'一生一次的事件需要一生一次的消费'来为婚礼上的超额开销辩护，相比之下别的品类不会这样。结果是零售市场出现了双层定价。这个我们听说过，CBC 也报道过，是真实存在的：婚礼版商品比平时的同款要加价——

turns.en: Think like floral arrangements for a wedding versus a non-wedding event. This begs the big question, which is, is the tendency to spend more on wedding-related items benefiting the future of your relationship, to spending more, make for a better wedding or, more importantly, to make for a better marriage?
turns.zh: 比如婚礼上的花艺和非婚礼场合的花艺。这就引出大问题：为婚礼相关物品多花钱，真的对你关系的未来有益吗？多花钱，婚礼会更好吗？更重要的是——婚姻会更好吗？

turns.en: This is where the findings from this paper are super interesting. They have survey data from over 3,000 married survey participants, and they find that after controlling for variables like income, demographic, and other relationship factors, that the opposite is true.
turns.zh: 这正是那篇论文发现有趣的地方。他们用了 3,000 多名已婚者的调查数据，在控制了收入、人口统计和其他关系因素之后，发现情况恰恰相反。

turns.en: Higher engagement ring spending was linked to a greater risk of divorce among men, and higher wedding spending was linked to greater risk of divorce among women.
turns.zh: 订婚戒指花得越多，男性离婚风险越高；婚礼花得越多，女性离婚风险越高。

turns.en: Wedding-related debt stress might have been one possible mechanism. Who experienced the lowest divorce rate spent less than $1,000 on their wedding, which is just fascinating.
turns.zh: 婚礼债务压力可能是其中一个机制。离婚率最低的那对夫妇，婚礼花费不到 1,000 美元——这太让人着迷了。

turns.en: Personally, my wedding cost around $300 back in 2013. It's a very small wedding outside in Ottawa. It was awesome. And I'm still married. How many guests?
turns.zh: 就我个人而言，2013 年我的婚礼大概花了 300 美元。就在渥太华办的户外小婚礼，非常棒，我现在还结着呢。来了多少位？

turns.en: It was my sister, Tessa, my parents, and my wife. There you go. And that's it. Could kind of pull this back to the tightwad spendthrift continuum.
turns.zh: 我妹妹 Tessa、我父母，加上我太太。就这样。

turns.en: I don't think anybody would argue that the pressure to spend more on, I don't know about rings, but certainly on weddings has increased a lot over the last 10, 15 years, whatever period.
turns.zh: 就这样啊。这事可以拉回到'抠门—挥霍'的连续谱上。我觉得没人会否认，不说戒指，起码婚礼的开支压力在过去 10、15 年大幅增加。

turns.en: People who are more inclined to be tightwads now have a lot more pressure on them if they want to resist that. And people who are inclined to be spendthrift kind of have free reign to indulge that now because you can spend an awful lot on a wedding without kind of judgment that you might have had to endure in years past or without the kind of judgment you might endure if you spent that money on something other than a wedding.
turns.zh: 倾向抠门的人现在要抵抗，压力更大；倾向挥霍的人现在反而有了放开手脚的空间，因为婚礼花很多钱几乎不会受到过去那种评判，也不会像把钱花在其他东西上那样引人议论。

turns.en: So I think if you have a conflict between a tightwad and a spendthrift partner, you're going to see it clash pretty heavily when you're planning the wedding.
turns.zh: 所以，如果伴侣一个是抠门者、一个是挥霍者，筹备婚礼时会是一次正面冲撞。

turns.en: Yeah. It would be a very good early first test. If you've got a spendthrift that wants to do a flashy wedding and a tightwad that wants to do it as fiscally responsible as possible, how you handle that discussion will set the tone for the marriage.
turns.zh: 是的。那会是婚姻早期非常好的一次'压力测试'。一个想办得风光的挥霍者，加一个想尽量财务负责的抠门者——怎么处理那场讨论，会奠定婚姻的基调。

turns.en: But more importantly, I think the social pressure on that couple is going to be much more difficult to endure for the tightwad. For sure. Yeah, because it's become such an accepted, normal, expected even thing to do.
turns.zh: 更重要的是，我觉得那股社会压力对抠门的一方要难承受得多。因为大手大脚办婚礼已经成了被接受的、正常的、甚至理所当然的事。

turns.en: Exactly. I always look back at my wedding and I'm like, yep, glad we did it that way. I did not do my wedding as cheap as you did, Ben, but I was pretty close.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我回头看自己的婚礼，总说：好，我们那样办是对的。我的婚礼没你的那么便宜，Ben，但也差得不远。

turns.en: Going to the engagement ring, I went the sentimental route. I bought a gold ring and I knew my wife had a diamond ring from her grandmother that she wanted to be incorporated.
turns.zh: 再说订婚戒指，我走的是情感路线。我买了一枚金戒指，因为我太太有一枚祖母传下来的钻石戒指，她希望把它融进去。

turns.en: My wife will tell you a funny story that I went and stole the ring from her parents' house, which is not completely true. I had permission anew, but they weren't home.
turns.zh: 我太太可以讲那个趣事：我从她父母家把戒指'偷'了出来——也不完全算偷，我确实得到了许可，只是他们人不在家。

turns.en: I used the garage code to go grab the ring at the time and then turned it into a beautiful ring for her. I wanted to do the traditional thing of asking her parents to have her hand in marriage and at that point, they like, so you came in and took the ring and it was pretty funny.
turns.zh: 我用他们车库的门禁密码进去拿的戒指，然后把那枚戒指改造成了一枚漂亮的新戒指。我本来想按传统方式向她父母请求把女儿嫁给我，到那会儿他们——'你就走进来把戒指拿走了？'回想起来挺好笑的。

turns.en: It was pretty funny to look back on, but then our wedding was not crazy expensive. I think it was maybe 5,000 total, but we got 150 people like mostly family and some friends.
turns.zh: 不过回想起来确实好笑。我们婚礼也不贵，总共 5,000 美元左右，来了 150 人，大多是家人和一些朋友。

turns.en: We used as many free options we had. We had a free photographer, someone gifted a DJ, we had a friend who made cakes and favors, so we saved money as much as possible and I don't regret doing it the way we didn't.
turns.zh: 我们用了所有能免费用的资源：免费的摄影师，有人送了 DJ，朋友做了蛋糕和伴手礼，尽最大可能省钱。我一点也不后悔那样办。

turns.en: May also be a reflection of the time, like we didn't have much money. We got married relatively young, but I don't regret doing that and don't think we missed out.
turns.zh: 也许也反映当时的情况——我们那时候没什么钱，比较年轻就结了。但我不后悔，也不觉得错过了什么。

turns.en: We had a great time and lots of good memories. The other counterintuitive finding from this study is that there were two types of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages in this sample.
turns.zh: 我们玩得开心，留下了很多好回忆。这项研究还有一个反直觉的发现：有两种婚礼支出反而预测了更长的婚姻。

turns.en: One was having more guests at the wedding and the other was going on a honeymoon in both cases regardless of the price. It kind of shows that a wedding and honeymoon don't need to be and I would argue should not be shows of wealth, but they can still be great experiences.
turns.zh: 一种是婚礼宾客多，一种是去度蜜月，两者都与价格无关。这说明婚礼和蜜月不需要——我认为也不应该——是炫富，但依然可以是很棒的体验。

turns.en: You shouldn't go broke buying a ring and you don't want to max out a credit card on a wedding venue, but there are still ways to do. I mean, having a nice honeymoon and having lots of people you care about at your wedding without having to spend a whole bunch of money, if that's even possible, having a whole bunch of people together at a venue, if anyone gets a hint that it's a wedding, it's going to
turns.zh: 你不必为了戒指破产，也不该为了婚礼场地刷爆信用卡。但仍然有办法：蜜月可以很好，你在乎的人可以都到场，还不用花很多钱——如果那还可能的话。一大群人聚在场地里，只要透出'这是婚礼'的风声，就会更贵。

turns.en: get more expensive. Yeah. Well, I had 150 people at my wedding and did it for $5,000, had a buffet, no open bar, worked pretty well. Yeah, that's good.
turns.zh: 对，我 150 人的婚礼，5,000 美元办完，自助餐、没有开放酒吧，效果就很好。不错。

turns.en: This one's one of my favorites, I think, on this topic because I remember when I was early in my financial planning career and I would spend a lot of time talking to young couples, this is always one of the first questions I would get asked is how should we structure our finances?
turns.zh: 这个话题我觉得是我最喜欢的之一。我记得刚进入财务规划行业那会儿，花很多时间和年轻夫妻聊，他们问我的头几个问题里总有：我们该怎么安排财务？

turns.en: Should we have joint accounts? Should we combine our finances? Should we have separate finances? It seems like this pretty innocuous financial decision, but I can actually have a huge impact on your financial life and just tons of potential answers.
turns.zh: 要不要开共同账户？要不要把钱合到一起？要不要分开管理？看起来是个温和的财务小决定，但它其实能对你的财务生活产生巨大影响，答案可以千奇百怪。

turns.en: I've seen every possible combination of bank accounts that you can think of for a couple, but what tends to work best, the evidence is pretty strong, which is that couples should manage their finances together.
turns.zh: 夫妻银行账户的组合方式，我能想到的都见过。但往往最管用的——证据相当强——是夫妻共同管理财务。

turns.en: Some of the research does suggest that means joint accounts, but some of it suggests it doesn't necessarily have to be, but the main idea is that combining finances has some pretty clear benefits.
turns.zh: 一些研究说的是要开共同账户，另一些觉得不一定非要这样。但核心是：合并财务有一些相当明确的好处。

turns.en: There's one 2022 analysis across six studies and more than 38,000 participants that finds that couples who fully pooled their finances reported greater relationship satisfaction and were less likely to break up, which held cross-culturally, which is interesting.
turns.zh: 2022 年一项分析汇总了 6 项研究、超过 38,000 名参与者，发现完全合并财务的夫妻报告的关系满意度更高，也更不容易分手，

turns.en: The 2023 study in the Journal of Consumer Research found that joint accounts promoted communal norms, shared goals, and better feelings about managing money as a team, which are all linked to greater relationship and life satisfaction.
turns.zh: 而且跨文化都成立，很有意思。2023 年 Journal of Consumer Research 的研究也发现，共同账户促进了共有规范（communal norms）、共同目标，以及'作为一个团队管钱'的良好感受——这些都与更高的关系和生活满意度相关。

turns.en: Now, interestingly, this is the part that I mentioned that the benefits of combined finances may not even have to come as a consequence of actually combining finances, like using a joint account.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，这就是我说的部分：合并财务的好处，未必真的来自物理上的合并——用共同账户这件事。

turns.en: Simply thinking about your finances as combined can produce positive results, so the 2025 paper Talk About Shared Money, which is by Johanna Peetz, who was actually a guest on this podcast many years ago, she found that, well, yes, the act of pooling finances caused couples to communicate more openly and frequently about money, simply redirecting people's attention toward their existing joint accounts rather than their separate ones was enough
turns.zh: 仅仅把财务'视为'共同的就能产生正面效果。2025 年的论文《Talk About Shared Money》，作者 Johanna Peetz——她多年前其实来上过我们这个节目——她发现，合并财务这个行为确实让夫妻更坦诚、更频繁地聊钱；但仅仅是把受试者的注意力从各自的私人账户引导到已有的共同账户上，就足以

turns.en: to produce a similar effect. So I think couples who are thinking about their finances as ours rather than mine and yours tend to talk more and more productively about money, regardless of how the accounts are actually set up.
turns.zh: 产生类似的效果。所以我认为，把财务看成'我们的'而不是'我的和你的'的夫妻，往往聊得更多也更有效，无论账户实际怎么设置。

turns.en: And then the other big benefit in this, Dan, you alluded to when we first started talking to this topic, the other big benefit of combined finances is that the effect of combining finances seems to make the relationship between wealth and life satisfaction stronger, which is interesting.
turns.zh: 还有一个大好处——Dan，我们开始聊这个主题时你也提到过——合并财务似乎能强化'财富—生活满意度'之间的关系。这很有意思。

turns.en: So the 2022 paper, My Wealth, Your Life Satisfaction, which finds that increases in jointly held wealth led to greater life satisfaction, whereas gains in individually held wealth did not have any significant impact.
turns.zh: 2022 年的论文《My Wealth, Your Life Satisfaction》发现，共同持有的财富增加会带来更高的生活满意度，而个人持有的财富增加没有显著影响。

turns.en: Yeah. So then practically speaking, like you actually need to combine your finances, I don't know, in my household, we do everything in a main joint account.
turns.zh: 对。那从实操上说，你真的需要把财务合并吗？我们家所有钱都在一个主共同账户里。

turns.en: And that's it. Where everything happens, the research says it doesn't necessarily have to be that way. I think it's a pretty efficient way to do it, though.
turns.zh: 就这样，所有事都走那个账户。研究说未必非得这样，但我觉得这是一种相当高效的做法。

turns.en: But the main thing is thinking about finances jointly, even if they aren't physically or whatever, electronically joint. The joint accounting is going to be really important again, if you've got this kind of spendthrift tightwad dynamic going on.
turns.zh: 核心是共同地看待财务，哪怕它们在物理上、电子上没有并在一起。当然，如果存在'挥霍—抠门'的差异张力，共同记账就尤为重要。

turns.en: And again, I don't have any research to back this up, but my intuition tells me if the two partners, one was on the tightwad side and one was on the spendthrift side, the tightwad would probably be happier with separate accounts because they feel like they could build a little bit of a fence around kind of their account.
turns.zh: 这里我没有研究支撑，只是直觉：如果两个人一个偏抠门、一个偏挥霍，抠门的那位大概会更想要分开的账户，这样能给自己的账户围一圈小篱笆；

turns.en: And if their partner is inclined to spend more freely, then there's at least that separation. Whereas if both of them were on the contented side, or frankly, if they were both tightwads or both spendthrift, the joint account would be much easier.
turns.zh: 假如对方花钱比较奔放，那至少有一层隔离。而如果两人都偏'无冲突型'，或者两人都是抠门者，或者都是挥霍者，共同账户就容易得多。

turns.en: I think it would be difficult to share a joint account with someone who was at a very different part of that spectrum. The closer you are, the more likely the joint account seems to me to be the right way to go.
turns.zh: 我觉得和谱系上离得很远的人共用一个账户会很费劲。你俩越接近，共同账户看起来就越是对的选择。

turns.en: That's tough. And I think you're right. When you look at what the research on this says, it's you're less likely to have shared goals. Life satisfaction is decreasing, but it speaks again to just what the first piece of research that we talked about says, is that if you are on opposite ends of that tightwad spendthrift spectrum, it does lead to marital conflict and it does lead to lower marital satisfaction.
turns.zh: 这很难讲。我觉得你说得对。看这块的研究结论：如果你在这条'抠门—挥霍'谱系的两端，确实会导致婚姻冲突、更低的婚姻满意度——这又回到我们最开始那段研究说的，共享目标变少，生活满意度下降。

turns.en: And I think that you're kind of pointed out a practical mechanism. I agree with you. It probably does make sense to keep accounts separate if you're very different, but that's in itself a problem.
turns.zh: 你其实指出了一个现实的机制。我同意：如果差异很大，分开账户可能确实更明智——但那本身就是个问题。

turns.en: Many people, it doesn't have to be all the way one side or the other, right? I mean, I certainly know a lot of clients or other couples who have just shared, like they have a joint account for their joint expenses and then they each have their own account.
turns.zh: 很多人不用走到两个极端。我当然认识很多客户或别的夫妻是折中的：一个共同账户应付共同开支，然后各自再留一个自己的账户。

turns.en: People can be very mechanical about how much each has to contribute to the joint account each month, whatever, you can work that out among yourselves.
turns.zh: 人们可以很机械化地规定每人每月向共同账户贡献多少之类的事，总之你们自己可以商量着定。

turns.en: But for a lot of couples, that compromise makes sense. You know you have mostly shared expenses in the house, but each one feels like, you know what?
turns.zh: 但对很多夫妻来说，这种折中是合理的：你们知道家里基本都是共同开支，但每个人都想要一点自己能自由支配、不用对方查银行对账单的钱。

turns.en: I want a little bit of money that I can spend myself without you checking my bank statements. And depending on the relationship dynamic, I'm sure it can work well also.
turns.zh: 视关系动态而定，它也可以运作得很好。

turns.en: I agree. I think it comes down again to communication. Like if you agree, okay, you each have a budget of X amount per month to do what you wish with.
turns.zh: 同意。我觉得说到底还是沟通。如果你们达成一致：每人每月有 X 额度的自主预算——

turns.en: The tightwad saves most of it, the spend-thrift spends, then it's less likely it's going to cause conflict if you have agreed on principle. These are the guidelines for how we manage our finances and we'll save this much jointly than that can work.
turns.zh: 抠门的存下来，挥霍的花掉——既然原则上讲好了，就不太容易引起冲突：这是我们管钱的准则，我们共同存下这么多，这样可以运作。

turns.en: I find where if people have a joint view on how they manage their money, having additional accounts, not one way that's right or wrong, I think it just adds more mental overhead and complexity.
turns.zh: 我发现，如果两人在钱的看法上本来就一致，再加额外账户——无论哪种都没有对错之分——只是多了心智负担和复杂度。

turns.en: Like if you agree that what's ours is ours and if you have to move money from individual account to joint account and switch money all around, just adds more to think about.
turns.zh: 如果你们认同'我们的就是我们的'，却还要在个人账户和共同账户之间来回转钱、倒来倒去，就是多出了一堆要想的事。

turns.en: And if it works for you, then that's great, but there's other layers that you need to think about when you're setting up your joint banking.
turns.zh: 如果那种方式对你合适，那很好。但设置共同银行业务时，还有其他一些层面要考虑。

turns.en: I agree on that. It's all about communication. If my wife or I want to spend money on something substantial, we will just have a conversation about it rather than having a budget for stuff that we don't have to ask each other questions about.
turns.zh: 我同意这一点。都是沟通。我太太或我要花一笔大的，就直接互相商量，而不是划出一块'不用问对方'的预算。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I've heard of couples that have like a threshold, like anything over $500 or $1,000, we should talk about it first. It does start to lead into another topic that I want to talk about, which is financial infidelity, where I think talking about what works for a couple.
turns.zh: 对，正是这样。我听说过夫妻设一个门槛：超过 500 或 1,000 美元先商量。这其实引出了我想聊的下一个话题——金融不忠（financial infidelity）：聊聊什么对夫妻是管用的。

turns.en: If you do something that doesn't work, but you kind of agree to it, but one person doesn't really agree to it, but they say they do, then you end up with financial infidelity, which is not great.
turns.zh: 如果你做了不管用的事，表面上双方都同意了，其实有一方心里并不同意、只是嘴上说好——那就滑向了金融不忠，这不好。

turns.en: The definition of it is engaging in financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of and then hiding it. It's actually pretty common in marriage.
turns.zh: 它的定义是：做出你预期伴侣会反对的财务行为，然后把它们藏起来。这在婚姻中其实相当常见。

turns.en: There is a recent paper that looks at what happens when one partner is much more prone to it than the other. And couples with that kind of mismatch are more likely to end up with individualized rather than shared financial goals.
turns.zh: 有一篇较新的论文研究了一方的这种倾向远强于另一方时会发生什么。存在这种错配的夫妻，更可能形成个人化而非共享的财务目标。

turns.en: And this also predicts lower financial well-being and lower relationship satisfaction. And interestingly, this finding holds up even after accounting for other mismatches between partners like one being a tightwad and the other being a spendthrift.
turns.zh: 这也预示着更低的财务福祉和更低的关系满意度。有意思的是，在考虑了双方其他类型的错配之后——比如一个是抠门者、一个是挥霍者——这个结论仍然成立。

turns.en: That's of course hard to do if you stick to joint accounts. That is potentially one argument for joint credit card, joint bank account. And then you just have this understanding like, look, whatever I buy, my partner is going to see it.
turns.zh: 坚持共同账户的话，隐藏当然就很难了。这也许是支持共同信用卡、共同银行账户的一个论点：你心里明白，我买什么伴侣都会看到。

turns.en: I mean, if you want to buy gift or something, there's ways to do that and keep it a secret. But it'd be pretty hard to hide major spending chronically if you are only working with joint accounts.
turns.zh: 我是说，如果你想买个礼物，有的是办法保密。但如果只走共同账户，想长期隐藏大额消费就很难了。

turns.en: It's not to say that it's only appropriate if people don't trust each other. It's just a matter of transparency, not usually a bad thing. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这不是说只有互不信任的夫妻才该这样安排。它更多是一种透明——通常不是坏事。是啊。

turns.en: If there is transparency, but the case we're talking about here is financial infidelity. So if someone is intentionally trying to hide it, even if you started with a joint account, it could result in a separate hidden account being created and it could cause some serious conflict because it's no longer just finances.
turns.zh: 有透明是好事，但我们这里说的是金融不忠。如果一方刻意隐瞒，哪怕一开始用的是共同账户，也可能冒出隐蔽的私人账户，引发严重冲突，因为这已经不只是钱的问题了——

turns.en: You're breaching trust with your partner. So it could get messy pretty quick. I kind of think that birds are going to get flushed over regardless.
turns.zh: 这是对伴侣信任的背叛，会很快变得难收拾。我倒是觉得，纸终究包不住火。

turns.en: Like if someone's conducting financial infidelity and you say, all right, we're doing joint accounts, then they're either going to find another way to do it or it's just going to bring the issue to the forefront and you're going to get separated.
turns.zh: 如果有人铁了心搞金融不忠，你说'好，我们用共同账户'，要么他会找别的办法绕过去，要么问题直接被摆上台面，然后你们就分开了。

turns.en: It's a bigger problem than we can solve with our financial planning guidance. It's for the counselors or the divorce attorneys to deal with.
turns.zh: 那是大到不是我们的财务规划指引能解决的问题。那是婚姻咨询师或离婚律师要处理的事。

turns.en: Yeah. Whether finances are combined or joined, I think another big question that every couple grapples with, and we see this as financial advisors a lot.
turns.zh: 是啊。不管财务是合并还是分开，还有一个每对夫妻都会面对的难题，我们做财务顾问的经常看到——

turns.en: The other big question that households have to grapple with is how much each spouse should be involved in household financial decision making.
turns.zh: 就是每个配偶应该在多大程度上参与家庭财务决策。

turns.en: Again, as advisors, we see this all the time. It's very common for there to be a primary financial spouse, whereas the less financial spouse is sometimes not even super engaged in the financial conversation.
turns.zh: 同样，作为顾问我们太常见了：往往有一位主要财务配偶，另一位不怎么'财务'的一方，有时并不怎么参与财务讨论。

turns.en: You can have a lot of conversations that end up being dominated by one spouse and that can be with an advisor, but good financial advisor will try and check that and engage both spouses.
turns.zh: 很多对话最后由一方主导——和顾问聊天时也一样。好的财务顾问会设法纠正这一点，让两位配偶都参与进来。

turns.en: But I think if it's just the two people on their own, a lot of decisions can end up being dominated by one spouse. It's not because the concepts are too complicated for the other spouse to understand, but it can be difficult to step back and be objective about your own financial life without defaulting into how things are usually done.
turns.zh: 但如果只是夫妻两个人自己聊，很多决定容易被一方主导。不是因为概念对另一方太复杂难懂，而是很难跳出来、客观地看待自己的财务生活，不落入平时的惯性。

turns.en: If your spouse in any other direction just always makes these decisions or does stuff and tells you about it after the fact, then it's kind of hard to step back and say, well, hey, maybe we should approach this decision differently.
turns.zh: 如果总是配偶一方做所有决定，或者先做了再告诉你，你就很难退一步说：嘿，这个决定我们也许可以换个做法。

turns.en: And I do think that being mediated is not quite the right word, but being somewhat of a financial mediator or a neutral third party between couples does end up being a big part of what advisors at firms like PWL Capital do for couple clients is just a different conversation when there's a third party who's not part of the relationship in the room.
turns.zh: 用'mediated'（被调解）这个词不太准确，但作为夫妻之间某种财务中间人、一个中立的第三方，恰恰是 PWL Capital 这类公司的顾问为夫妻客户做的很重要的一部分——房间里有一个不属于这段关系的人在场，对话就是不一样。

turns.en: This does tend to point toward male dominated influence on important household decisions like asset allocation, a 2026 paper in the review of financial studies, those of the average Australian household incorporates 60% of the husband's risk tolerance, but only 40% of the wife's into the household level asset allocation.
turns.zh: 这往往指向重要家庭决策上更男性化的影响力，比如资产配置。2026 年 Review of Financial Studies 上的一篇论文发现：澳大利亚普通家庭在家庭层面的资产配置中，纳入了丈夫风险承受能力（risk tolerance）的 60%，却只纳入妻子的 40%。

turns.en: The other state that this implies a 20% point gap in bargaining power, a half of that gender gap is driven by observable characteristics like income and employment, and then the other half can be traced back to a gender effect as the authors describe it.
turns.zh: 这隐含了 20 个百分点的议价能力（bargaining power）差距。这一性别差距的一半由收入、就业等可观测特征驱动，另一半则可归因于作者所称的性别效应（gender effect）。

turns.en: The average bargaining power for husbands is 69% in Germany and 61% in the United States, but the authors do say that the three countries, Australia, Germany, and the US are statistically indistinguishable from each other in terms of husband bargaining power, but all of them are above 60%.
turns.zh: 丈夫的平均议价能力在德国是 69%，在美国是 61%。不过作者也说，澳大利亚、德国、美国三国的丈夫议价能力在统计上无法区分，但都超过 60%。

turns.en: What's most surprising here is that discounting a wife's financial input cannot be attributed solely to her lack of financial knowledge. The 2021 journal finance paper, Who Wears the Pants finds that US households with a financially sophisticated husband are more likely to participate in the stock market than households with a wife of equal financial sophistication, and the authors argue that this pattern is best
turns.zh: 最让人意外的是：贬低妻子的财务意见，并不能单纯归因于她缺乏金融知识。2021 年 Journal of Finance 的论文《Who Wears the Pants》（谁当家）发现，丈夫金融素养高的美国家庭，比妻子同等素养的家庭更可能参与股票市场，

turns.en: explained by gender identity norms rather than by differences in competence. They also run a randomized experiment in the paper, which points to the mechanism.
turns.zh: 作者认为这一模式最好用性别身份规范（gender identity norms）来解释，而不是能力差异。他们还在论文里做了一个随机实验，指向了机制：

turns.en: Female identity suppresses the wife's willingness to contribute ideas while male identity makes husbands less receptive to a spouse's input.
turns.zh: 被激活的女性身份会抑制妻子贡献想法的意愿，而男性身份让丈夫更难接纳配偶的意见。

turns.en: That paper is in the journal finance. It's interesting to have that topic covered in that journal, but there it is. A short 2018 conference paper by the same author extends the pattern internationally, that paper was just looking at the US.
turns.zh: 那篇发在 Journal of Finance 上。财经期刊会讨论这个话题挺有意思的，但事实如此。同一作者 2018 年一篇简短的会议论文把这一模式扩展到国际——刚才那篇只看了美国。

turns.en: The second conference paper, shorter conference paper, finds that households in countries with stronger traditional gender norms are less likely to participate in the stock market with suggestive evidence that the pattern holds among wealthy households as well.
turns.zh: 第二篇较短的会议论文发现：传统性别规范更强的国家，家庭参与股票市场的比例更低；而且有暗示性证据显示，富裕家庭中也存在这一模式。

turns.en: These norms carry a real financial cost through the stock market participation shell, which is really a shame given what we know about how the sex is actually traded differently in Barbara and Odin's 2001 study of 35,000 households with brokerage accounts.
turns.zh: 这些规范通过股市参与的落差带来实实在在的财务代价。结合我们对两性交易行为差异的了解，就更可惜了：Barber 和 Odean 2001 年研究了 35,000 个有经纪账户的家庭——

turns.en: Men traded 45% more than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence produces excessive, harmful trading. That activity in their study was costly.
turns.zh: 男性的交易频率比女性高 45%，与'过度自信（overconfidence）导致过度的、有害的交易'的预测一致。在他们的研究里，这种活跃是有代价的：

turns.en: Trading reduced men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points per year versus 1.72 percentage points for women. To be clear, both groups hurt themselves by trading too much.
turns.zh: 交易使男性的净回报每年减少 2.65 个百分点，女性减少 1.72 个百分点。说清楚，两组人都因为交易过多伤害了自己，

turns.en: Women just did less of it. Whatever the return consequences, I do think that a household that systematically discounts one spouse's preference is making decisions that only one of the two people actually endorses, and that seems worth fixing for its own sake.
turns.zh: 只是女性做得少一些。无论回报后果如何——我认为一个系统性地贬低一方偏好的家庭，做出的决定其实只有两个人中的一位真正认可，光这一点就值得修正。

turns.en: It's always hard to make generalizations, and I hesitate to do so, but I will say based on my experience working with client households, client couples mostly.
turns.zh: 做概括总是很难，我也很不愿意这样，但根据我服务客户家庭的经验——大多是一男一女的夫妻——

turns.en: I get a male-female couple. I would say the one who is my primary contact about the planning and investing is the woman as often as it is the man.
turns.zh: 我会说，在规划和投资上把我作为主要联系人的，是妻子的概率和是丈夫的一样高。

turns.en: I'd be shocked if it wasn't really close to 50-50, but to take it a step further, this idea about affecting stock market exposure is really interesting because I would say in the households where the man is more likely to be our primary contact, we talk more about the portfolio and more about investing, and in the households where the woman is primarily our contact, we spend more time talking about the planning.
turns.zh: 如果不是接近五五开我会很惊讶。再进一步，'这会影响股市敞口'这个点真的很有意思：在以丈夫为主要联系人的家庭里，我们聊组合、聊投资更多；在以妻子为主要联系人的家庭里，我们花更多时间聊规划。

turns.en: I haven't quantified this in any way, but that's my intuition, and I think that there is some social pressure on men who think that they need to know about markets and investing.
turns.zh: 我没有量化过，这只是我的直觉。我觉得社会上对男性有一种压力，让他们觉得自己必须懂市场、懂投资。

turns.en: In a way, they're expected to know about sports and cars. I don't know if this sounds like a stereotype, but to me, I see a little bit of that because from time to time, I will talk to a male client who I get the feeling is kind of bluffing, asking questions that he feels like he thinks he should ask, but it doesn't really feel honest.
turns.zh: 某种程度上，就像他们被期待懂体育和车一样。不知道这算不算刻板印象，但我确实看到一点：有时和男客户聊，我感觉他在虚张声势——问一些他觉得自己'应该问'的问题，但听起来不那么真诚。

turns.en: It feels a bit more performative. Were you almost never hear that? I never hear that from our female clients. Take that for what it's worth.
turns.zh: 更像是在表演。你几乎从没听到过这种情况吗？我从女性客户那里从没听到过。各位自己体会吧。

turns.en: That shows up in the financial literacy literature where men are more likely to be overconfident. They're more likely to confidently answer a question incorrectly, whereas women are more likely to say that they don't know the answer to the question, even if they actually did.
turns.zh: 这在金融素养文献中也有体现：男性更容易过度自信——会更自信地答错问题；女性则更倾向于说不知道答案，哪怕她其实知道，

turns.en: They tend to be underconfident. You're correct. I think that as an advisor, it's really important for you to try to be aware of that dynamic and do everything you can to bring both partners into the conversation whenever possible.
turns.zh: 更容易低估自己。你说得对。我觉得作为顾问，重要的是意识到这种动态，尽一切可能把伴侣双方都带进对话。

turns.en: You'll see it sometimes in a meeting, one spouse will be going on and on. You have to make the effort and turn to the other and say, what do you think?
turns.zh: 你有时在会议里会看到：一位配偶滔滔不绝，你必须刻意转向另一位问：你怎么看？你同意吗？

turns.en: Do you agree with that? Where are you coming from? Because it's something I think that just in general, trying to do a financial plan for a household is going to be a lot easier and a lot more satisfying for them if they both feel some ownership and some engagement in the process.
turns.zh: 你的出发点是什么？因为总的来说，如果家庭双方都对过程有拥有感和参与感，为这个家庭做财务规划会容易得多、满意度也高得多。

turns.en: That leads to such a better balanced conversation. Less dominant spouse tends to have a completely different perspective than the more dominated spouse and just gives different perspectives, planning, it's kids or trips or gifting or all these different things that can come up in financial planning conversations that would not necessarily be top of mind for the opposite spouse.
turns.zh: 这会带来平衡得多的对话。不太主导的那一方往往和主导方有完全不同的视角，带出很不一样的东西——规划对话里会出现孩子、旅行、赠与等各种话题，

turns.en: It's good to get both sides, whether you're doing it on your own. If you're a DIY investor, even if you are the main partner managing the portfolio, you're going to want to think about the more broad financial planning picture and include your spouse in those decisions and discussions.
turns.zh: 而这些未必是配偶另一方第一时间会想到的。所以两边的想法都要纳入。哪怕你自己做 DIY 投资，哪怕你是管组合的主要一方，你也要考虑更广的财务规划画面，把配偶纳入那些决策和讨论。

turns.en: I often hear, well, my spouse is just not interested. You don't have to be interested in the details of portfolio management and tax strategies to care about what's important to you.
turns.zh: 我经常听到：我配偶就是不感兴趣。但你不必对组合管理或税务策略的细节感兴趣，也可以关心对你来说重要的事。

turns.en: Your money is a means to do things, to achieve the goals that you want to achieve. Everybody cares about that to some extent. Being part of those conversations is important, even if you're not interested in the money aspect or the technical aspects of the conversation.
turns.zh: 钱是你做事、实现目标的手段，每个人多少都在意这一点。哪怕你对'钱'本身或对话的技术层面不感兴趣，参与那些对话也很重要。

turns.en: For sure. Continuity too, right, where if one spouse makes all the decisions and does not involve the other spouse and something happens to the primary financial spouse and they don't have an advisor, that can be very difficult for the spouse who's kind of been in the dark the whole time to carry on after the fact.
turns.zh: 没错。还有连续性：如果一方做所有决定、不带另一方参与，万一主要财务配偶出了什么事，又没请顾问——

turns.en: That's definitely a reason why we've had a number of clients come to us quite late in life and that's a very common reason why, where the one spouse who's been managing the finances will come to us and say, I'm just concerned about what might happen if I go first.
turns.zh: 这对一直蒙在鼓里的那位太难了。这绝对是我们不少客户很晚才来找我们的常见原因：

turns.en: My partner would not be able to manage on their own and then you feel like the sharks are going to start circling. The bank's going to call you.
turns.zh: 一直管钱的那位会说：'我担心如果我先走了，我的伴侣没办法自己打理。'然后你会感觉'鲨鱼'开始围过来，银行会打电话给你——

turns.en: And they will, is the thing. So they're like, I just want to know that if it's not me, somebody I trust is looking after my family. It's very responsible, I think, for a person to be that humble, but also that forward thinking and not in denial that at some point that could happen.
turns.zh: 而且他们真的会打，这就是问题所在。对方说：'我只想知道，如果我不在了，有一个我信任的人在照顾我的家人。'我觉得一个人能如此谦逊、如此有远见、不逃避'总有一天可能发生'的现实，是非常负责任的。

turns.en: It's usually a good time to reach out. Yeah, we definitely do see people reaching out for that reason that there was a really interesting paper a few years ago now that showed that there can be significant issues with cognitive decline that goes unnoticed, leading to poor financial decisions.
